title: MB5-02166
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). He is claiming refugee protection under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
The allegations in support of this claim are found in the claimant's Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) and can be summarized as follows:

The claimant alleges that he fears being arrested, tortured or killed by the authorities in his country for having reported corrupt police officers and their wrongful deeds XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country.
He held various positions with XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country. First, in 1966, he was the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and supervised XXXX who monitored XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

Between 19XXXX and 19XXXX, he was responsible for XXXX XXXX. He held various positions in other cities, and from 19XXXX to 2006, he worked as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX From 2006 to 2014 he was the [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX."

The claimant describes his duties in recent years as follows:1 [translation] 7. Despite my advancement in rank, I continued to perform the duties of XXXX advisor. My work had two aspects, a XXXX aspect and an administrative aspect. As part of these duties, I advised management about the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and, when there was a problem with XXXX XXXX XXXX, I was sent to document the problem. I also wrote reports about XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

He alleges that, during the inspection of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in 2003, he discovered fictitious XXXX XXXX-deserters-listed on the payroll, and he issued a report on XXXXfictitious XXXX out of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. On XXXX XXXX, 2003, there was an attempt on his life in XXXX and he was shot in the XXXX.

In 20XXXX, during the crackdown on members of the Bundu-dia-Congo, he acted as XXXX advisor, gathering testimony from victims in order to submit a report to his superiors. During his investigation, it was determined that Rwandans XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX were responsible for mass killings. Following the report, he was suspended with pay from 20XXXX to 20XXXX.

In XXXX 2013, when the authorities clamped down on the kulunas, gangs of delinquents, summary executions were carried out by the authorities, and two police officers involved told him about the wrongful deeds against the kulunas. The claimant reported those facts to the UDPS opposition party, to the national association of migrant and women's rights, to the UN, to Human Rights Watch and to the UN, which wrote a scathing report2 against the Congolese authorities.

With regard to his leaving the DRC for Canada, the claimant wrote that on or about XXXX XXXX, 2014, a group of police officers under the orders of General Kanyama went looking for him at his home in the morning in order to arrest him as a result of his reporting police abuses against the groups of delinquents.
Since he feared General Kanyama, he fled his home and restricted his movements because he thought that his life was in serious danger in XXXX 2014.

A friend helped him to obtain his American visa in XXXX 2015. He explained his delay in leaving the DRC after he obtained his American visa as follows: since he wanted to leave the country without being arrested by the authorities, his friend helped him to find good contacts so that he could get through the Kinshasa airport and leave his country.
He left the DRC on XXXX XXXX, 2015, for Chicago, United States. He entered Canada at Fort Erie on April 26, 2015,3 and claimed refugee protection that same day.

The claimant alleges in his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) that he had been XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country since 19XXXX and that his last position XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country was [translation] "XXXX XXXX XXXX." A notice of exclusion under 1F(a) and (c) was sent to the Minister in accordance with the requirements of rule 26.4

On November 25, 2015, the Minister sent the panel a written notice of intervention.5 The Minister is asking the panel to reject the claimant's the refugee protection claim, submitting that his claim lacks credibility.
In his notice of intervention, the Minister is not asking that the claimant be excluded.

According to the evidence on record, the claimant arrived in Canada on May 26, 2015 (not on April 26, 2015), with his Congolese passport and the American visa he had obtained in XXXX 2015; certified copies of these are on record.6
After verifying the said documents in his presence, his identity was established.
The claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under sections 96 or 97 of the Act.
The determinative issue in this refugee protection claim is the credibility of the claimant's story, which the panel did not believe for the following reasons.
In its decision, the panel also considered the documents provided by the claimant's counsel after the hearing.7 CREDIBILITY

The claimant is a 74-year-old man whose physical movements are very slow. He speaks slowly but he expresses himself well, and he understood very well the questions put to him by the panel and his counsel at the hearing.
Nevertheless, his answers were often evasive, even when they were very simple and clear.

His narrative and testimony contain discrepancies, contradictions and major implausibilities that have undermined his credibility regarding his story of fear and persecution from the authorities in his country.

According to the panel, if the claimant was sought by the authorities in his country since XXXX 2014, they would not have promoted him in 2015, given his allegation that he had been suspended from 20XXXX until his departure from his country.
Moreover, he did not claim asylum in the United States, where he stayed from XXXX to May 2015, and he did not provide any reasonable explanation. The claimant's promotion XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

First, according to the evidence, the claimant was promoted8 as XXXX XXXX XXXX by the president and prime minister of his country on XXXX XXXX, 2015, yet he stated that he had been suspended by XXXX authorities since XXXX 20XXXX because he had written a report incriminating high-ranking XXXXofficials.

The claimant wrote in his narrative that he has been suspended from 20XXXX to present, which he confirmed in his testimony. The panel therefore asked him to explain how he could have been promoted by an order of the president and the prime minister of his country on XXXX XXXX, 2015.9

He told the panel that he had three theories to suggest: a) his suspension in 20XXXX was made only verbally; b) he had lodged an appeal in 20XXXX challenging his lack of promotion; c) he suspected it was a trap laid by the authorities in order to arrest him.
When the claimant was questioned by the Agency on this same topic, he proposed a fourth theory-the fact that the authorities were not aware that he had been suspended in XXXX 20XXXX.

The claimant stated that, while he was suspended, he had to go to sign in each week in order to receive his pay, because he was on stand-by. In his testimony, he stated that he went to sign in twice a week! Therefore, there were written signs in his file indicating that he had been suspended.

Even considering the particular context of a country like the DRC, the panel cannot explain how a high-ranking XXXX such as the claimant-XXXX advisor to the XXXX XXXX, no less-could have been suspended by his superiors with only a verbal notice to this effect from 20XXXX to today.
Moreover, how does one explain that the president and the prime minister of the country granted a promotion to a high-ranking XXXX XXXX without the recommendation of his superiors?

To justify his promotion in XXXX 2015, despite his allegation that he was sought by the police in his country since XXXX XXXX, 2014, and had to leave his country secretly on XXXX XXXX, 2015, without any trouble from those same authorities, the claimant's explanation is so illogical and implausible that the panel grants it no credibility.

The claimant has not established that he was suspended and persecuted by the authorities in his country because of his activities XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country, or that he would be in the future.
The panel read the UN report on the kulunas written by the UN in 2014. That report does not establish that the claimant faces a risk in his country because the sources are anonymous.

Moreover, as his counsel indicated, the reports from international organizations, like the UN, never identify their sources. If the claimant was the source of the information in the October 2014 UN report, as his counsel states in his last exhibit, the authorities in his country would not know this.

As for the supposed incriminating report written by the claimant in 20XXXX, he did not provide the panel with evidence to corroborate his testimony. He also failed to give a reasonable explanation as to why he was suspended yet promoted in 2015 by the authorities in his country. Moreover, if he did write an incriminating report that he submitted to his superiors, then the authorities in his country have been in possession of that report for a long time, so it is no longer a secret held by the claimant. Departure from the DRC in XXXX 2015
According to the claimant, he had to leave his country secretly in XXXX 2015, and he was living in hiding because he had feared the authorities in his country since XXXX 2014.
Moreover, he stated that he had been living in hiding and restricted his movements since XXXX 2014 because he was afraid of being arrested or killed by General Kanyama, whose abuses he had denounced.

Yet, the claimant left his country in XXXX 2015 using his own passport and, according to his own testimony, he was issued an authorization for departure by the police authorities in his country in order to go to the United States in XXXX 2015.

When the panel asked him to explain how he had managed to obtained an authorization to leave the DRC if he was sought since XXXX 2014, he answered that his friend had helped him get the authorization to leave his country and obtain the American visa.

In the claimant's BOC Form, he states that his friend had helped him with leaving the Kinshasa airport, as he did not want to be arrested by the authorities, not with obtaining an American visa, as he stated in his testimony.

The panel does not find it credible that a high-ranking XXXX XXXX in the DRC who was sought by the police in his country could have left with his own identity documents, even if the panel considers the widespread corruption in that country.

Moreover, in his testimony, the claimant clearly stated that the authorities were aware that he was travelling abroad to receive medical treatment. So, this was not a secret departure from the country, contrary to what the claimant stated. Political fear and ethnicity

The claimant alleges that he also fears persecution by reason of his ethnicity and his political membership in the opposition party, the UDPS. His answers were vague and evasive, even when the questions were simple.

For example, the panel asked him whether he was a member of the UDPS opposition party. He hesitated for a long time; he first answered that he was a supporter, then stated that he had been a member since the party was founded in 1982; then, in answer to his counsel's question, he replied that XXXX XXXX were not authorized to be members of political parties in the DRC.

The panel asked him why he did not obtain evidence from the UDPS regarding his collaboration in writing the reports and evidence of said reports from 2013 and 2014 denouncing the activities of the police in his country. Again, he alleged that he had to leave the country secretly and quickly.

The panel did not believe that the claimant left his country in XXXX 2015 without the knowledge of the authorities there. Without any evidence to corroborate the alleged persecution due to reports incriminating the XXXX XXXX, the panel did not believe the claimant.

On the contrary, the evidence supposedly indicates that the claimant had been a high-ranking member of XXXX XXXX XXXX in his country since 19XXXX. He worked with XXXX XXXX in various cities, including XXXX from 19XXXX to present. He was promoted to XXXX XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX, 2015, by the president and prime minister of the DRC.10 The claimant was more a part of the country's state apparatus than an opponent to that apparatus.

Moreover, at question 9 in his Schedule A form, he gives no indication that he was a member of the UDPS, but he did indicate the Red Cross. The evidence does not establish that the claimant was a political opponent in the DRC.

The claimant further stated for the first time at the hearing that he fears persecution by reason of his ethnicity. He is a member of the Luba tribe, which is often associated with opponents of the current Kabila regime.

According to the evidence, the claimant was a high-ranking XXXX XXXX in his country by his own acknowledgement. The evidence does not allow for a conclusion that the claimant was or would be persecuted by reason of his ethnicity.

The claimant stated that he fears returning to his country because he is a XXXX XXXX According to the evidence, the claimant stated that the authorities are aware that he went abroad for medical treatment. Consequently, he has not established that he could not prove this if he returned to the DRC. Late claim and delay in leaving the DRC

Lastly, the panel notes that the claimant obtained his American visa on XXXX XXXX, 2015, and that he left his country on XXXX XXXX, 2015, although he stated that he had been in hiding since XXXX 2014 and had decided at that time to leave the DRC.
The panel asked him why he did not leave before XXXX 2015. He answered that he was avoiding being captured by the police.

As noted by the panel earlier, it did not believe that the claimant was sought by the authorities in his country. If that had been the case, he would have used the visa he obtained in XXXX to leave the DRC. This further undermines his credibility.

Furthermore, he stayed in the United States from XXXX XXXX to May 26 without claiming asylum. When asked to explain why, he answered that his friends had advised him to come to Canada; he was not interested in claiming asylum in the United States, and that DRC authorities often travel to the United States.

The panel notes that the claimant's daughter lives in Canada, which could have explained his decision to claim refugee protection in Canada, but he did not mention this to the panel. The other three explanations given by the claimant are not reasonable. He stayed in the United States for XXXX months before coming to file his claim here. If the claimant feared persecution in the DRC and had left his country because of that, he would have claimed asylum in the United States.

The lack of a claim in the United States and the lack of a reasonable explanation for not filing a claim for asylum in a country that is a signatory to the Convention, just as Canada is, adds to the other factors that undermine the claimant's credibility.

The claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection" under sections 96 or 97 of the Act, because he did not establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, nor any risk under to subsection 97(1) if he were to return to the DRC.

The refugee protection claim is rejected.
